abstract:
Background: bronchial asthma is a highly
heterogeneous
chronic inflammatory disease, with eosinophilic (EA) and neutrophilic
(NEA) asthma subtypes exhibiting distinct pathological mechanisms
and treatment responses. However, the protein-metabolite interactions
underlying the pathogenesis of asthma remain poorly understood, limiting
the development of precision diagnostics and therapeutics. Methods: this study integrated proteomics, metabolomics,
and bioinformatics analyses to perform multiomics profiling of sputum
samples from 53 asthma patients (27 EA, 20 NEA) and 53 healthy controls.
Differential expression analysis, weighted gene coexpression network
analysis (WGCNA), and CIBERSORT immune cell infiltration analysis
were systematically applied to characterize the molecular features
of EA and NEA. Machine learning approaches (LASSO regression, SVM-RFE,
and Random Forest) were further employed to screen biomarkers and
construct diagnostic models. Results: the study systematically
characterized proteins and metabolites in asthma patients and healthy
controls. We constructed comprehensive interaction networks that reveal
critical protein–metabolite relationships and dysregulated
pathways, elucidate potential molecular mechanisms underlying asthma
heterogeneity, including inflammatory signaling cascades, oxidative
stress responses, and metabolic reprogramming. The study also revealed
that EA is characterized by Th2-type immune responses and dysregulated
histidine/purine metabolism, whereas NEA exhibits neutrophil-mediated
oxidative stress (HIF-1 signaling activation, arginine metabolism
disturbance) and predominant innate immunity. Multiomics network analysis
identified reactive oxygen species (ROS) metabolism and cytokine production
as key features in EA, while hypoxia response and NF-κB pathway
enrichment were prominent in NEA. A diagnostic model based on 7 core
proteins (ASS1, C4B, etc.) effectively distinguished asthma from healthy
controls (AUC = 0.944), while 2 overlapping biomarkers (CLCA1, NAMPT)
accurately stratified EA and NEA (AUC = 0.903). Conclusion: this study comprehensively delineated the distinct immune-metabolic
signatures of asthma patient and healthy controls, as well as EA and
NEA through multiomics integration and to establish high-accuracy
noninvasive diagnostic models. These findings provide novel targets
for molecular subtyping and precision treatment of asthma, particularly
offering a theoretical foundation for hypoxia-pathway-targeted interventions
in NEA.

Methods
2.1
Study Design and Participant Selection
This single-center
observational study was conducted to investigate
proteomic and metabolomic in bronchial asthma. A total of 53 bronchial
asthma and 53 healthy controls were recruited from The First Affiliated
Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University between May 2024 and May
2025. Asthma diagnosis followed the GINA guidelines,
according to fulfilment of 1 or more of the following criteria:
(1) an increase >12% in forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1)
and
an increase >200 mL after inhalation of 400 μg of albuterol;
(2) a 20% reduction in FEV1 in response to a provocative concentration
of inhaled methacholine (PC20 < 10 mg/mL); (3) and/or an increase
>20% in FEV1 after 2 weeks of treatment with systemic oral corticosteroids
(OCS) or inhaled corticosteroids (ICS). (4) Participants were aged
between 18 and 70 years. (5) All study participants attended a single
visit that encompassed assessments of lung function, asthma symptoms,
asthma-specific quality of life, and medication use, with no history
of smoking. (6) Patients were initially diagnosed with mild-to-moderate
asthma exacerbation or persistent asthma according to GINA guidelines.
(7) Patients had been routinely treated with fluticasone or an equivalent
dose of ICS for over 6 months but had experienced more than 1 acute
exacerbations in the past half year.
Exclusion criteria:
history of chronic lung diseases or any other diagnosed conditions,
ongoing immunotherapy, malignancy diagnosis, recent respiratory infection,
or antibiotic use in past 4 weeks.
Healthy controls were age-
and sex-matched individuals without respiratory symptoms, recent infections,
or chronic respiratory diseases. All controls demonstrated normal
pulmonary function tests and had no history of systemic antibiotic
use within the preceding 4 weeks. A schematic representation of the
study can be found in
Figure
.
1
Integrated multi-omics analysis for bronchial asthma investigation.
Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee
of The
First Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University (approval
codes: 2022 No. 121 and 2024 No. G-007). Written informed consent
was obtained from all participants before study enrollment, and the
study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
2.2
Samples Collection
Sputum induction
involved isotonic saline with a bronchodilator, processed as described
in ref
. Asthma
patients were classified as EA or NEA based on sputum cell counts:
EA had ≥3% eosinophils; NEA had <3%
eosinophils and neutrophil thresholds of ≥75.57% (<20 years),
≥61.61% (20–40 years), ≥63.25% (40–60
years), or ≥67.25% (>60 years). Samples with >10% squamous
cells were excluded. All participants underwent spirometry per ERS
guidelines to assess lung function and airway obstruction severity.
2.3
Liquid Chromatography–Mass Spectrometry
Analysis for Proteomics
Prior to LC–MS analysis, protein
samples (5 μL) underwent denaturation in 8 M urea/100 mM ammonium
bicarbonate (Sigma-Aldrich) in a 50 μL final volume. Sequential
reduction (10 mM DTT, 37 °C, 30 min) and alkylation (50 mM IAA,
RT, dark) preceded overnight tryptic digestion (1:30 enzyme/substrate,
37 °C; Promega). Digested peptides were purified using C18 StageTips
(Thermo Fisher) and quantified via Nanodrop One (A280). Chromatographic
separation employed a 15 cm × 75 μm C18 column (2 μm
particles; Dr. Maisch) with a 60 min 2–90% ACN/0.1% FA gradient
at 300 nL/min flow rate.
Mass spectrometric analysis data were
acquired using a timsTOF Pro2 (Bruker, Germany) in parallel accumulation-serial
fragmentation (PASEF) mode. The diaPASEF scan covered an
m
/
z
range of 400–1200, ion mobility 0.7–1.43
V s/cm
2
, with a 32 × 25 Th window scheme and 100 ms
ramp time. Raw data were processed using Spectronaut 18 (Biognosys),
targeting the UniProtKB human protein database. Applying the following
search criteria: tryptic specificity (≤2 missed cleavages),
carbamidomethylation (fixed), oxidation/acetylation (variable), and
strict mass accuracy thresholds. MS/MS spectra were interference-corrected,
with FDR controlled at <1% for both PSM and protein identifications.
2.4
UHPLC–MS/MS Analysis for Metabolomics
The metabolomic profiling protocol commenced with sample preparation
wherein 100 μL aliquots were combined with 400 μL of chilled
methanol (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) at a 1:4 (v/v) ratio. Following thorough
vortex mixing, complete metabolite extraction was achieved through
60 min ice-bath sonication. Subsequent protein precipitation was performed
via 1 h incubation at −20 °C, followed by centrifugation
(14,000
g
, 20 min, 4 °C) to obtain protein-free
supernatants. These supernatants were subsequently concentrated to
dryness using a Thermo Fisher Scientific vacuum concentrator prior
to LC–MS analysis.
The metabolomic analysis was performed
on an ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography–electrospray
ionization-quadrupole-Orbitrap mass spectrometry (UHPLC–ESI-Q-Orbitrap-MS)
system, specifically utilizing a Shimadzu Nexera X2 LC-30AD high-performance
liquid chromatography (HPLC) system (Shimadzu Corporation, Japan)
coupled with a Q-Exactive Plus mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific,
USA). Chromatographic separation was achieved using an ACQUITY UPLC
HSS T3 column (2.1 × 100 mm, 1.8 μm particle size, Waters
Corporation, USA), with a mobile phase of 0.1% formic acid in water
(Sigma-Aldrich, USA) (A) and 100% acetonitrile (Sigma-Aldrich, USA)
(B), flowing at 0.3 mL/min. The gradient program started at 0% B,
increased to 48% B over 4 min, then to 100% B over the next 4 min,
held at 100% B for 2 min, and returned to 0% B in 0.1 min, followed
by a 3 min re-equilibration phase.
For heated electrospray ionization
(HESI), the optimized settings
were: spray voltage at 3.8 kV for positive mode and 3.2 kV for negative
mode, capillary temperature at 320 °C, sheath gas flow at 30
arbitrary units, auxiliary gas flow at 5 arbitrary units, probe heater
temperature at 350 °C, and an S-Lens RF level of 50. Full MS
scans covered an
m
/
z
range of 70–1050
Da, with a resolution of 70,000 for full scans and 17,500 for MS/MS
scans at
m
/
z
200. Stepped normalized
collision energies (20, 30, 40) were used for fragmentation.
Quality control (QC) samples, made from pooled aliquots of all
specimens, and blank samples (75% acetonitrile in water, Sigma-Aldrich,
USA) were injected every six samples to ensure data integrity and
normalization consistency. MS-DIAL software was used for data analysis,
including peak alignment, retention time correction, and peak area
extraction. Metabolite identification was based on exact mass (tolerance
<10 ppm) and MS/MS spectral data (tolerance <0.02 Da), using
databases such as Human Metabolome Database (HMDB), MassBank, and
a proprietary metabolite standard library. Only metabolites detected
in over 50% of samples in any group were considered for further analysis,
ensuring the reliability and significance of detected metabolites.
2.5
Construction of Weighted Gene Coexpression
and Immune Infiltration Analysis
To explore the complex genetic
interactions and identify potential biomarkers or therapeutic targets
for asthma, we employed the Weighted Gene Coexpression Network Analysis
(WGCNA) framework using the “WGCNA” package in R software
(version 4.4.2).
The input data comprised
a proteomic expression matrix derived from LC–MS analysis.
To ensure robust analysis and minimize spurious correlations, the
data underwent rigorous preprocessing. Low-abundance proteins with
expression variance in the lowest 25% quartile were filtered out to
prioritize biologically informative proteins. Proteins with missing
values in >50% of all samples were first filtered out to ensure
data
reliability. For the remaining missing values, median imputation was
applied, where each missing value was replaced by the median expression
level of the corresponding protein across all samples. The ‘goodSamplesGenes̀’
function confirmed data quality. A soft-thresholding power (β
= 18) was selected using ‘pickSoftThreshold̀’,
achieving a scale-free topology fit (
R
2
> 0.85) while balancing network connectivity. A topological overlap
matrix (TOM) was constructed from a Pearson’s correlation-based
adjacency matrix, and modules were identified via hierarchical clustering
with a minimum size of 30 proteins. The gray module, containing proteins
with weak coexpression, was excluded from downstream functional analyses
to ensure biological interpretability. Gene modules were identified
using average linkage hierarchical clustering based on TOM-based dissimilarity,
and modules significantly associated with asthma were selected for
further exploration.
For immune cell infiltration analysis,
we performed computational deconvolution of proteomic data using established
R packages. The source code of the R package was obtained from the
official CIBERSORTx Web site (
https://cibersortx.stanford.edu/
). We employed the CIBERSORT algorithm to quantify the relative abundances
of 22 immune cell subsets in sputum proteomic profiles, comparing
asthma patients versus healthy controls, and EA versus NEA subgroups.
2.6
Proteomics Statistical Analysis
Statistical
analysis of proteomics data was performed using Perseus software and
R software. The analysis encompassed hierarchical clustering at both
the protein and peptide levels, with sequence annotation supported
by databases such as UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes
and Genomes (KEGG), and Gene Ontology (GO). Enrichment analyses for
GO terms and KEGG pathways were conducted using Fisher’s exact
test, with multiple comparisons controlled via false discovery rate
(FDR) correction. GO terms were categorized into biological processes
(BP), molecular functions (MF), and cellular components (CC), with
pathways deemed statistically significant at a
q
-value
threshold of <0.05.
Additionally, furthermore, protein–protein
interaction (PPI) networks were constructed using the STRING database
and visualized with Cytoscape software to elucidate functional relationships
among differentially expressed proteins (DEPs). Hub protein analysis
was performed within the Cytoscape environment, identifying the top
10 hub proteins through the minimum concave cost (MCC) algorithm and
the top 8 hub proteins using the molecular complex detection (MCODE)
algorithm. Then we employed a Venn diagram approach that combined
hub proteins identified by WGCNA, DEPs, MCC, and MCODE algorithms,
enabling systematic prioritization of key hub proteins for subsequent
immune infiltration analysis.
2.7
Metabolomics
Statistical Analysis
To distinguish between the metabolic
profiles of subjects, we constructed
models based on orthogonal partial least squares-discriminant analysis
(OPLS-DA). The robustness and predictive accuracy of these models
were assessed using permutation tests (
n
= 200) to
ensure against overfitting. Model quality was evaluated based on R2X
(cumulative) and R2Y (cumulative) values, which reflect the descriptive
power of the model, and Q2 (cumulative) values, which indicate predictive
reliability. Ideal models achieved values close to 1 for these metrics.
Importantly, for a model to be considered valid, the
R
2
and
Q
2
values obtained from
permutation tests must not exceed those of the original, nonpermuted
model, confirming that predictive capabilities are not due to chance.
The identification of discriminating metabolites was based on variable
importance in projection (VIP) values from the OPLS-DA model, coupled
with a two-tailed Student’s
t
-test applied
to normalized data for univariate analysis. Additionally,
p
-values were determined using one-way analysis of variance
(ANOVA) for comparisons involving multiple groups. Fold-change (FC)
values were calculated based on the mean values for each patient group,
with selection criteria for differentially expressed metabolites (DEMs).
Visualization tools such as volcano plots, heat maps, and boxplots
were employed to represent these findings, using the ‘heatmap’
and ‘ggplot2’ packages in R software (version 4.4.2).
Further, KEGG pathway analysis was performed to explore the biological
implications of the identified DEMs, utilizing the Metaboanalyst6.0
web portal (
http://www.metaboanalyst.ca/
).
2.8
Statistical Analysis
2.8.1
Statistical
Analysis of Clinical Data
Statistical analyses of clinical
indices were conducted using SPSS
software (version 26.0). Continuous variables were expressed as mean
± standard deviation (SD) for normally distributed data or as
median with interquartile range (IQR) for non-normally distributed
data. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Between-group
comparisons were conducted using independent
t
tests
for normally distributed variables and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for
non-normally distributed variables, and a
p
-value
of <0.05 was set as the threshold for statistical significance.
2.8.2
Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve
Validation
The diagnostic performance of each identified
hub protein was evaluated using ROC curve analysis with the “pROC”
package in R software. This analysis provided estimates of the area
under the curve (AUC) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Biomarkers
with an AUC greater than 0.8 were considered diagnostically relevant,
serving as a reliable measure of each gene’s capacity to distinguish
between disease states.
2.8.3
Machine Learning Analysis
Three
machine learning approaches were employed for predictive modeling
and biomarker discovery: (1) random forest (RF) for feature importance
evaluation and variable selection, (2) support vector machine (SVM)
for high-dimensional classification, and (3) least absolute shrinkage
and selection operator (LASSO) regression to identify the most predictive
protein associations strongly linked to asthma pathogenesis. The data
set was split into a training set (75%,
n
= 80, including
40 asthma and 40 healthy controls) and a validation set (25%,
n
= 26, including 13 asthma and 13 healthy controls) using
stratified random sampling to maintain balanced representation of
asthma and control groups. For EA versus NEA stratification, the asthma
cohort (
n
= 47) was similarly split into a training
set (75%,
n
= 35, including 20 EA and 15 NEA) and
a validation set (25%,
n
= 12, including 7 EA and
5 NEA). LASSO regression was performed with 5-fold cross-validation
repeated 10 times to select features with nonzero coefficients. SVM-RFE
employed 5-fold cross-validation repeated 10 times during the recursive
elimination process to rank features until the root-mean-square error
(RMSE) was minimized. For the RF model, hyperparameters were optimized
through 10-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times, using 500 trees
(ntree), unlimited tree depth, and 3 features considered at each split
(mtry = 3), and ranking features by mean decrease in Gini impurity.
The intersection of features identified by all three methods was used
to construct logistic regression models. Model performance was evaluated
using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, with
the area under the curve (AUC) and 95% confidence interval (CI) reported
for both the training and validation sets.

1
Introduction
Bronchial asthma is a
prevalent and debilitating chronic respiratory
disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of wheezing, breathlessness,
chest tightness, and coughing, affecting over 300 million individuals
worldwide.
,
This complex disease manifests through persistent
airway inflammation, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and reversible
airflow obstruction, with pathogenesis involving intricate interactions
between genetic predisposition and environmental triggers.
,
The underlying mechanisms encompass multiple pathological processes,
including Th2-mediated eosinophilic inflammation,
Th17-driven neutrophilic activation,
oxidative stress-induced airway remodeling,
and impaired epithelial barrier function.
Notably, emerging evidence highlights the crucial role
of metabolic reprogramming and microbiome dysbiosis in modulating
immune responses and disease severity.
,
Despite
significant advances in asthma management, substantial
challenges persist in clinical practice. Eosinophilic asthma (EA)
and neutrophilic asthma (NEA) represent two predominant inflammatory
endotypes with distinct pathogenic mechanisms and clinical characteristics.
Studies have demonstrated that EA is primarily driven by Th2-mediated
immune responses and eosinophilic airway inflammation, which typically
responds well to corticosteroid therapy.
In contrast, NEA is predominantly mediated through Th17/IL-23 axis
activation, featuring neutrophil-dominant inflammation and oxidative
stress bursts, with approximately 40–50% of patients exhibiting
corticosteroid resistance.
Current therapeutic
strategies, primarily relying on inhaled corticosteroids and bronchodilators,
demonstrate limited efficacy in approximately
30–50% of patients, particularly those with neutrophilic subtypes.
This therapeutic gap stems largely from the
remarkable heterogeneity of asthma, which encompasses diverse endotypes
and phenotypes with distinct molecular signatures and treatment responses.
This therapeutic gap underscores the urgent
need for precise endotyping strategies to identify NEA-specific molecular
signatures and therapeutic targets.
With the rapid advancement
of omics technologies, our research
capabilities in understanding asthma pathogenesis have undergone revolutionary
improvements. The systems biology approach integrating proteomics
and metabolomics has become a powerful tool in biomedical research,
,
particularly in biomarker discovery and precise phenotyping of complex
diseases. Through comprehensive analysis of the interrelationships
between metabolites and proteins, we can understand biological processes
from holistic, dynamic, and multidimensional perspectives,
thereby facilitating the identification of robust
molecular signatures for disease classification. This integrated research
methodology has been widely applied in the field of traditional medicine
and has demonstrated remarkable potential in screening diagnostic
biomarkers and establishing molecular subtyping systems.
Regarding
biomarker development, the Global Initiative for Asthma
(GINA 2023) guidelines have recommended blood eosinophil counts (≥300
cells/μL) and fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO ≥50
ppb) as auxiliary diagnostic indicators for EA.
However, the specificity of these markers significantly
decreases in patients with comorbid allergic diseases. For NEA diagnosis,
although biomarkers such as YKL-40 and IL-17 have demonstrated moderate
predictive value in Western populations,
validation studies in Asian cohorts showed significantly reduced
diagnostic performance.
Therefore, deciphering
the molecular signatures of these distinct endotypes and establishing
reliable biomarkers for early diagnosis are critically important for
precision asthma management.
This study systematically elucidates
immunometabolic signature
differences between bronchial asthma and healthy controls by integrating
large-scale proteomic, metabolomic, and machine learning approaches.
Comparisons between asthma patients and healthy controls provide foundational
context for understanding core molecular alterations, while endotype-specific
analyses identify key immune-inflammatory and metabolic pathways distinguishing
EA and NEA. Our machine learning-derived diagnostic model successfully
discriminates between these endotypes, offering a robust tool for
precise subtyping and laying the groundwork for personalized asthma
management.
This study employs an integrated multiomics approach
to investigate
asthma patients and healthy controls, particular further differentiating
between eosinophilic (EA) and neutrophilic (NEA) asthma endotypes.
Through systematic protein and metabolite characterization, differential
expression analysis, and computational modeling, we constructed comprehensive
interaction networks that reveal critical protein–metabolite
relationships and dysregulated pathways. These networks elucidate
potential molecular mechanisms underlying asthma heterogeneity, including
inflammatory signaling cascades, oxidative stress responses, and metabolic
reprogramming. The work ultimately aims to identify key molecular
signatures and validate potential biomarkers for improved asthma subtyping
and personalized therapeutic strategies.

Additionally, furthermore, protein–protein
interaction (PPI) networks were constructed using the STRING database
and visualized with Cytoscape software to elucidate functional relationships
among differentially expressed proteins (DEPs). Hub protein analysis
was performed within the Cytoscape environment, identifying the top
10 hub proteins through the minimum concave cost (MCC) algorithm and
the top 8 hub proteins using the molecular complex detection (MCODE)
algorithm. Then we employed a Venn diagram approach that combined
hub proteins identified by WGCNA, DEPs, MCC, and MCODE algorithms,
enabling systematic prioritization of key hub proteins for subsequent
immune infiltration analysis.
2.7
Metabolomics
Statistical Analysis
To distinguish between the metabolic
profiles of subjects, we constructed
models based on orthogonal partial least squares-discriminant analysis
(OPLS-DA). The robustness and predictive accuracy of these models
were assessed using permutation tests (
n
= 200) to
ensure against overfitting. Model quality was evaluated based on R2X
(cumulative) and R2Y (cumulative) values, which reflect the descriptive
power of the model, and Q2 (cumulative) values, which indicate predictive
reliability. Ideal models achieved values close to 1 for these metrics.
Importantly, for a model to be considered valid, the
R
2
and
Q
2
values obtained from
permutation tests must not exceed those of the original, nonpermuted
model, confirming that predictive capabilities are not due to chance.
The identification of discriminating metabolites was based on variable
importance in projection (VIP) values from the OPLS-DA model, coupled
with a two-tailed Student’s
t
-test applied
to normalized data for univariate analysis. Additionally,
p
-values were determined using one-way analysis of variance
(ANOVA) for comparisons involving multiple groups. Fold-change (FC)
values were calculated based on the mean values for each patient group,
with selection criteria for differentially expressed metabolites (DEMs).
Visualization tools such as volcano plots, heat maps, and boxplots
were employed to represent these findings, using the ‘heatmap’
and ‘ggplot2’ packages in R software (version 4.4.2).
Further, KEGG pathway analysis was performed to explore the biological
implications of the identified DEMs, utilizing the Metaboanalyst6.0
web portal (
http://www.metaboanalyst.ca/
).
2.8
Statistical Analysis
2.8.1
Statistical
Analysis of Clinical Data
Statistical analyses of clinical
indices were conducted using SPSS
software (version 26.0). Continuous variables were expressed as mean
± standard deviation (SD) for normally distributed data or as
median with interquartile range (IQR) for non-normally distributed
data. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Between-group
comparisons were conducted using independent
t
tests
for normally distributed variables and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for
non-normally distributed variables, and a
p
-value
of <0.05 was set as the threshold for statistical significance.
2.8.2
Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve
Validation
The diagnostic performance of each identified
hub protein was evaluated using ROC curve analysis with the “pROC”
package in R software. This analysis provided estimates of the area
under the curve (AUC) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Biomarkers
with an AUC greater than 0.8 were considered diagnostically relevant,
serving as a reliable measure of each gene’s capacity to distinguish
between disease states.
2.8.3
Machine Learning Analysis
Three
machine learning approaches were employed for predictive modeling
and biomarker discovery: (1) random forest (RF) for feature importance
evaluation and variable selection, (2) support vector machine (SVM)
for high-dimensional classification, and (3) least absolute shrinkage
and selection operator (LASSO) regression to identify the most predictive
protein associations strongly linked to asthma pathogenesis. The data
set was split into a training set (75%,
n
= 80, including
40 asthma and 40 healthy controls) and a validation set (25%,
n
= 26, including 13 asthma and 13 healthy controls) using
stratified random sampling to maintain balanced representation of
asthma and control groups. For EA versus NEA stratification, the asthma
cohort (
n
= 47) was similarly split into a training
set (75%,
n
= 35, including 20 EA and 15 NEA) and
a validation set (25%,
n
= 12, including 7 EA and
5 NEA). LASSO regression was performed with 5-fold cross-validation
repeated 10 times to select features with nonzero coefficients. SVM-RFE
employed 5-fold cross-validation repeated 10 times during the recursive
elimination process to rank features until the root-mean-square error
(RMSE) was minimized. For the RF model, hyperparameters were optimized
through 10-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times, using 500 trees
(ntree), unlimited tree depth, and 3 features considered at each split
(mtry = 3), and ranking features by mean decrease in Gini impurity.
The intersection of features identified by all three methods was used
to construct logistic regression models. Model performance was evaluated
using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, with
the area under the curve (AUC) and 95% confidence interval (CI) reported
for both the training and validation sets.

While previous studies have delineated the protein-metabolite interaction
networks in bronchial asthma compared to healthy controls, the clinical
management of asthma remains challenging due to the divergent therapeutic
responses across inflammatory phenotypes. Among these, EA and NEA
represent two predominant but mechanistically distinct subtypes, the
underlying protein-metabolite crosstalk remain poorly elucidated.
We performed an integrated multiomics analysis to unravel the dysregulated
molecular networks and interaction mechanisms distinguishing EA from
NEA, aiming to identify phenotype-specific diagnostic markers.
In our proteomic profiling of sputum samples from 53 bronchial asthma
patients, we stratified the asthma cohort into distinct inflammatory
endotypes, identifying 27 cases of EA and 20 cases of NEA based on
sputum cell counts. DEPs were identified using the following screening
criteria: |log
2
FC| > 1 and
q
-value
<0.05.
We identified 248 DEPs: 67 were upregulated, and 181 were downregulated
(
Figure
A, Supporting
Information
Table S15
). Through comprehensive
GO and KEGG pathway analyses, DEPs in critical biological processes
significantly enriched in core neutrophil functions (chemotaxis, degranulation,
bacterial killing), Fcγ receptor-mediated phagocytosis, reactive
oxygen species (ROS) generation. KEGG analysis further identified
significant enrichment in the Fc epsilon RI, VEGF, and HIF-1 signaling
pathways, demonstrating the critical involvement of immune hyperresponsiveness,
oxidative stress, and hypoxia-related pathways in asthma pathogenesis
(
Figure
B,C, Supporting
Information
Table S16
). A hierarchical
clustering dendrogram of the proteomic data effectively segregated
the 47 study samples, scale-free coexpression network. Pearson method
was used to establish the association between function and modules
(
Figure
D,E). Through
dynamic tree-cutting analysis, the coexpression network was systematically
partitioned into 8 distinct modules. Notably, one module exhibited
significant coexpression patterns of proteins. Through integrative
analysis of DEPs and WGCNA-derived modules significantly associated
with NEA, we identified 23 overlapping genes (
Figure
F). Functional characterization demonstrated
that these genes enriched in oxidative stress modulation, metabolic
rewiring, and oxygen-sensing mechanismsall hallmarks of neutrophilic
airway inflammation. The specific involvement of arginine metabolism
and HIF-1 signaling provides mechanistic insight into NEA’s
distinct pathophysiology compared to EA (
Figure
G, Supporting Information
Table S17
). The convergence of these pathways points to potential
therapeutic targets for modulating neutrophilic airway inflammation.

pyridine, xanthine) within the interaction network revealed significant
enrichment in several critical metabolic pathways, butanoate metabolism,
purine metabolism, nitrogen metabolism, taurine and hypotaurine metabolism,
arginine biosynthesis. These findings provide important mechanistic
insights into the distinct pathophysiological characteristics of EA
and NEA (
Figure
G,H).
3.9
Diagnostic Models for Differentiating Bronchial
Asthma and Inflammatory Phenotypes
To address the diagnostic
and stratification challenges posed by the clinical heterogeneity
of bronchial asthma, we employed machine learning approaches to identify
hub genes and construct two diagnostic models: one to distinguish
bronchial asthma from healthy controls, and another to stratify patients
into eosinophilic asthma (EA) and noneosinophilic asthma (NEA) subtypes.
We applied three machine learning algorithms for feature selection.
LASSO regression with 10-fold cross-validation identified 11 candidate
proteins (
Figure
A),
while SVM-RFE analysis indicated that the root-mean-square error (RMSE)
was minimized when 51 proteins were included (
Figure
B). The random forest algorithm screened
36 potential biomarkers (
Figure
C). By integrating the results from all three methods,
seven hub proteinsASS1, C4B, CHAD, CKM, MSLN, NAMPT, and PEBP4were
ultimately selected (
Figure
D,E). A logistic regression model based on these biomarkers
demonstrated strong discriminatory performance, with an AUC of 0.944
(95% CI: 0.884–0.979) in the training set and 0.928 in the
validation set (
Figure
F).

4
Discussion
This study provides a comprehensive
characterization of the molecular
signatures distinguishing bronchial asthma patients from healthy controls,
as well as between EA and NEA asthma subtypes, through an integrative
multiomics approach combining proteomics, metabolomics, and machine
learning. We constructed comprehensive interaction networks that reveal
critical protein–metabolite relationships and dysregulated
pathways. A well-constructed diagnostic model was established to discern
asthma from healthy individuals and to distinguish EA from NEA. These
findings not only confirm established aspects of asthma pathophysiology
but reveal novel immunometabolic networks and potential therapeutic
targets that could transform precision medicine approaches for this
complex disease.
4.1
Molecular Signatures and
Immunometabolic Networks
in Bronchial Asthma
Our proteomic analysis identified 1286
DEPs, with significant enrichment in oxidative phosphorylation and
antigen presentation pathways. These findings align with emerging
evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic reprogramming
in asthmatic airways.
,
The WGCNA revealed that the blue
module (positively correlated with asthma) was enriched for glutathione
metabolism and phagosome pathways, suggesting that impaired antioxidant
defenses may exacerbate oxidative damage through ROS accumulation.
,
Metabolomic profiling further demonstrated that disturbances in
β-alanine and histidine metabolism were closely associated with
enhanced Th2 inflammation, where histamine metabolites may amplify
immune responses via mast cell-epithelial cell axis activation.
These findings collectively support the emerging
paradigm of “immune-metabolic crosstalk” in asthma pathogenesis.
The comparative analysis between EA and NEA uncovered more profound
mechanistic differences. EA demonstrates a Th2-polarized phenotype
characterized by dysregulated histamine metabolism, where histidine
decarboxylase upregulation drives a self-amplifying inflammatory loop
through histamine-mediated Th2 cell proliferation and mast cell-derived
IL-4/IL-13 production.
This histaminergic
axis may explain the suboptimal response to current biologics in approximately
30% of EA patients.
In contrast, NEA
exhibits hypoxia-driven pathophysiology, with HIF-1α activation
promoting neutrophil survival while simultaneously inducing corticosteroid
resistance via NF-κB crosstalk.
,
Concurrent
disturbances in arginine metabolism further exacerbate airway hyperresponsiveness
through altered nitric oxide homeostasis,
highlighting fundamental differences in the molecular mechanisms
between these asthma endotypes.
4.2
Immune
Microenvironment and Cellular Crosstalk
CIBERSORT analysis
revealed endotype-specific immune landscapes.
The overall asthma phenotype showed increased NK cell activation and
reduced M2 macrophages, indicating dysregulated innate immunity that
may impair inflammation resolution.
The
coordinated elevation of eosinophils and activated CD4+ T cells in
EA reinforces the central role of the “Th2-eosinophil axis”,
while NEA demonstrated predominant M0 macrophage/mast cell accumulation,
reflecting innate immunity-driven pathology.
Notably, we identified
significant correlations between hub proteins and immune cells. IDH2
and APOB showed negative correlations with M0 macrophages, suggesting
their potential role in modulating macrophage polarization through
lipid metabolism regulation.
In NEA,
the positive correlation between ALPL, NOS2/3 and activated NK cell
simplifies possible involvement of oxidative stress-vascular tone
dysregulation.
These findings open new
avenues for therapeutic strategies targeting immunometabolic networks.
4.3
Clinical Implications of Multiomics Networks
The protein–metabolite interaction network derived from
our multiomics analysis reveals several clinically actionable therapeutic
targets that address the fundamental pathophysiological mechanisms
underlying different asthma endotypes. The consistent dysregulation
of FcεRI signaling and glutathione metabolism across asthma
subtypes
supports the expanded use of
anti-IgE therapies and antioxidant strategies in broader asthma populations,
with FcεRI expression levels potentially serving as a predictive
biomarker for treatment response.
For EA, our network analysis identifies histidine metabolism as a
pivotal regulatory node, representing a novel therapeutic target.
Preclinical studies have demonstrated that pharmacological inhibition
of histidine decarboxylase significantly attenuates eosinophilic inflammation
and airway hyperresponsiveness,
while
showing synergistic therapeutic effects when combined with existing
anti-IL-13 biologics.
This finding suggests
promising opportunities for developing combination therapies targeting
both the histaminergic and IL-13 pathways in EA.
In NEA, our
data highlight the therapeutic potential of simultaneously
targeting the HIF-1/NF-κB/arginase axis. Experimental evidence
indicates that combined inhibition of HIF-1 and NF-κB signaling
pathways markedly reduces neutrophilic inflammation and restores corticosteroid
sensitivity in NEA models.
Furthermore,
modulation of arginine metabolism through supplementation has been
shown to provide additional therapeutic benefits, supporting the development
of multitarget intervention strategies for this treatment-resistant
asthma phenotype.
These findings
collectively establish a molecular framework for
advancing precision medicine approaches in asthma management. By targeting
the distinct pathogenic networks operative in different asthma endotypes,
these strategies promise to overcome the limitations of current uniform
treatment paradigms and improve outcomes for patients with difficult-to-treat
asthma. Future clinical trials should focus on validating these targeted
approaches and developing companion diagnostics to identify patients
most likely to benefit from specific therapeutic interventions.
4.4
Diagnostic Model Performance and Limitations
Our machine learning diagnostic models demonstrated excellent performance
(AUC >0.9), outperforming conventional biomarkers like blood eosinophil
counts.
The integration of LASSO, SVM–RFE,
and random forest algorithms identified robust biomarkers with strong
clinical translation potential. C4B, as a key component of the complement
system, exhibits altered levels that may reflect increased susceptibility
to respiratory infections in asthma patients.
Furthermore, the two novel biomarkers (CLCA1 and NAMPT) identified
by our EA/NEA stratification model demonstrated strong mechanistic
links to fundamental pathogenic pathwaysCLCA1’s association
with histamine-mediated inflammatory cascades
and NAMPT’s involvement in hypoxia-response signaling networks,
thereby providing clinically actionable tools
for endotype-specific asthma diagnosis and management.
However,
sample size limitations and metabolite stability issues require validation
in larger multicenter cohorts. We fully acknowledge that the cohort
size in our study is relatively modest compared to certain previous
publications, which may affect the generalizability of the findings.
Nonetheless, the robust performance of our diagnostic modelseven
with this initial cohorthighlights the potential clinical
relevance of the identified biomarkers. Future large-scale, multicenter
studies are essential to further validate and refine these molecular
signatures. Building upon our findings, several critical research
avenues warrant further investigation. Experimental validation of
the HIF-1/arginine axis in preclinical models could elucidate its
therapeutic potential for neutrophilic asthma,
while parallel efforts to develop rapid point-of-care assays
for identified biomarkers like ALPL and APOB would facilitate clinical
implementation.
,
Importantly, the distinct molecular
signatures we identified strongly support the need for precision clinical
trials specifically designed to target different asthma endotypes.
Collectively, this work not only provides the most comprehensive molecular
characterization of asthma heterogeneity to date but also establishes
a robust foundation for advancing personalized therapeutic strategies
in asthma care.
5
Conclusion
This
study leverages an
integrative multiomics approach, combining
proteomic, metabolomic, and immune profiling, to delineate the molecular
pathogenesis of bronchial asthma, with a focus on EA and NEA endotypes.
While confirming established paradigmssuch as Th2-mediated
inflammation with elevated IgE and eosinophil activation in EA and
HIF-1 signaling with neutrophilic inflammation in NEAour analyses
reveal novel insights into protein-metabolite interactions, including
dysregulated histidine metabolism in EA and arginine/proline metabolism
in NEA. Machine learning algorithms identified robust diagnostic biomarkers
(CLCA1, NAMPT) with exceptional discriminatory capacity (AUC >
0.9)
for asthma classification and endotype stratification. These findings
advance the molecular understanding of asthma heterogeneity, uncover
novel immunometabolic networks, and provide a foundation for precision
medicine through targeted therapeutic strategies and biomarker-driven
diagnostics.
